les: Te klein om te sien, groot genoeg om siek te maak
kaps_punt: Die verband tussen kieme en siektes en die rol van Louis Pasteur.

items.bewering: Te klein om te sien, groot genoeg om siek te maak
items.bron: Merriam-Webster Medical, 'germ': 'a microorganism causing disease: a pathogenic agent (such as a bacterium or virus)' (https://merriam-webster.com/medical/germ). Microorganisms are by definition too small to see individually without a microscope.

items.bewering: Mense kon sien dat siekte van mens tot mens versprei, maar nie wat dit oordra nie.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory' (https://www.worldhistory.org/Germ_Theory/): contagion between people was described long before germ theory (Fracastoro, 16th century, used the word 'contagion'), while the agent remained unknown until the 19th century.

items.bewering: Daarom het hulle siekte dikwels aan slegte lug of aan 'n straf toegeskryf.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory' (https://www.worldhistory.org/Germ_Theory/): miasma theory, 'bad air' poisoned by decomposing matter; and 'a person's sins resulted in contracting a disease or illness as a punishment from the gods or God'.

items.bewering: Baie mense het ook geglo dat klein lewende dinge vanself uit dooie stof ontstaan.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory' (spontaneous generation, from Aristotle onward, that living organisms could spring from non-living matter); Penn State Microbiology 201, 'Spontaneous Generation' (https://psu.pb.unizin.org/microb201/chapter/spontaneous-generation/): still widely held when Pasteur tested it.

items.bewering: Louis Pasteur was 'n Franse wetenskaplike wat in die 1860's hierdie geloof getoets het.
items.bron: Britannica, 'Louis Pasteur: Spontaneous generation' (https://www.eb.com/biography/Louis-Pasteur/Spontaneous-generation, via search excerpt; the full page returned 403); Penn State Microbiology 201 ('In 1862, the great French scientist Louis Pasteur tested the validity of a widely held belief in spontaneous generation'). The work started in 1859 and was published in 1861-1862, with the Alhumbert Prize in 1862, so 'in die 1860's' is accurate for the experiments the lesson describes.

items.bewering: Hy het vloeistof in glasflesse gegiet. Daarna het hy die vloeistof in die flesse gekook om die klein lewende dinge daarin dood te maak.
items.bron: Memorial University Biology, 'Pasteur Swan-Neck' (https://www.mun.ca/biology/scarr/4270_Pasteur_experiment.html): broth placed in flasks and boiled to sterilise it.

items.bewering: By party flesse kon die lug met sy stoffies by die vloeistof kom. Daardie vloeistof het troebel geword en vrot geraak. By ander flesse kon die stoffies nie by die vloeistof kom nie, en dieselfde vloeistof het skoon gebly.
items.bron: Memorial University Biology, 'Pasteur Swan-Neck'; Penn State Microbiology 201. In the swan-neck flasks air still reached the broth but dust and microbes were trapped in the bend, and the broth stayed clear. Where the neck was broken or tilted, dust reached the broth and it clouded. The lesson keeps this distinction (only the dust was kept out, not the air), so it does not teach that air itself causes the spoilage.

items.bewering: Die bederf het dus van buite gekom en nie uit die vloeistof self nie.
items.bron: Penn State Microbiology 201; Memorial University Biology: the conclusion was that microbes come from existing microbes in the air and do not arise from the broth ('Omne vivum ex vivo').

items.bewering: Die flesse het oor bederf gegaan en nie oor siekte nie.
items.blok: Van vrot kos na 'n siek mens
items.bron: Memorial University Biology; Penn State Microbiology 201: the flask experiments tested spontaneous generation in broth (spoilage), not disease. World History Encyclopedia dates Pasteur's formal germ theory of disease to 1878, later.

items.bewering: Pasteur en ander wetenskaplikes het van daar verder gedink.
items.blok: Van vrot kos na 'n siek mens
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory': Pasteur and Koch 'are credited with the discovery of the germ theory in the 1860s-1880s', and Lister also built on it.

items.bewering: Klein lewende dinge kan kos en wyn laat bederf.
items.blok: Van vrot kos na 'n siek mens
items.bron: Britannica, 'pasteurization' (https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/446003/pasteurization, via search excerpt): in the 1860s Pasteur showed that abnormal fermentation (spoilage) of wine and beer was caused by microbes and could be prevented by heating; Wikipedia, 'Pasteurization' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteurization).

items.bewering: Sulke dinge kan dan ook in 'n mens se liggaam kom en hom siek maak. Dit is die verband tussen kieme en siekte.
items.blok: Van vrot kos na 'n siek mens
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory'; Merriam-Webster Medical, 'germ'.

items.bewering: Kieme is baie klein lewende dinge wat 'n mens siek kan maak. 'n Enkele kiem is te klein om met die blote oog te sien.
items.blok: Van vrot kos na 'n siek mens
items.bron: Merriam-Webster Medical, 'germ' ('a microorganism causing disease'). For a person: 'germ' commonly includes viruses, and whether viruses count as living things is a matter of definition among scientists. It is not a settled falsehood, and the dictionary sense ('microorganism') supports 'lewende dinge'. The lesson's 'kan' avoids saying that every small living thing causes disease. 'n Enkele (single) germ is microscopic; colonies can be seen, but the lesson rightly speaks of one germ.

items.bewering: Daardie verband het 'n nuwe manier gebied om siekte te voorkom. 'n Mens kon kieme weghou of hulle doodmaak.
items.blok: Van vrot kos na 'n siek mens
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory': Lister found that microbes caused wounds to rot and introduced washing instruments for each patient, which 'caused a noticeable decrease in deaths in surgical wards'. That is killing germs and keeping them away.

items.bewering: Op 'n houer vars melk in jou eie huis staan dikwels dat die melk gepasteuriseer is.
items.bron: South African Regulations relating to the Classification, Packing and Marking of Dairy Products (R. 1510 of 2019, Agricultural Product Standards Act), regulation 29(4), via acts.co.za (https://shop.acts.co.za/agricultural-product-standards-act-1990/r1510_29__additional_particulars_on_.php): where milk has been heat treated, the processing method must appear on the main panel near the class designation. Fresh milk sold in shops in South Africa is pasteurised, so the label says so.

items.bewering: Daardie melk is warm gemaak om die skadelike kieme daarin dood te maak. Daarna hou die melk langer en is dit veiliger om te drink.
items.bron: Wikipedia, 'Pasteurization' (heat kills pathogens and most spoilage organisms, extending storage time; milk at about 72 °C for 15 seconds or 63 °C for 30 minutes); Britannica, 'pasteurization'. Note: bacterial spores mostly survive pasteurisation. The standard public-health description, 'kills harmful bacteria', matches the lesson's level and is not false at Grade 6.

items.bewering: Hierdie metode is na Pasteur vernoem.
items.bron: Britannica, 'pasteurization' ('It is named for the French scientist Louis Pasteur, who in the 1860s demonstrated that abnormal fermentation of wine and beer could be prevented by heating'). The lesson does not claim that Pasteur first applied it to milk, which would be false. He first applied it to wine.

items.bewering: Pasteur het nie kieme ontdek nie.
items.bron: Smithsonian Ocean (https://ocean.si.edu/node/110415) and New World Encyclopedia, 'Anton van Leeuwenhoek' (https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek): microorganisms including bacteria were first observed by Van Leeuwenhoek in the 1670s.

items.bewering: Ander mense het hulle meer as honderd jaar voor hom onder 'n mikroskoop gesien.
items.bron: Smithsonian Ocean; New World Encyclopedia: Van Leeuwenhoek observed 'animalcules' (including bacteria) in 1675-1676 with his own microscopes. That is about 185 years before Pasteur's experiments of 1859-1862, so 'meer as honderd jaar' holds, and the plural 'ander mense' is safe (Hooke confirmed the observations).

items.bewering: Hy het ook nie alleen bewys dat kieme siekte veroorsaak nie.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory': Pasteur and Koch 'are credited with the discovery of the germ theory in the 1860s-1880s', and Koch's work 'all but settled the ongoing debate about germs being the cause of disease'.

items.bewering: Sy proewe het gewys waar bederf vandaan kom. Daarmee het hy die idee versterk dat kieme siekte veroorsaak.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory' ('Pasteur's work on the emerging germ theory disproved the earlier theory of spontaneous generation'); Penn State Microbiology 201.

items.bewering: Hy het later entstowwe teen siektes van diere en teen hondsdolheid gemaak.
items.bron: Britannica summary, 'Louis Pasteur' (via search excerpt): vaccines against chicken cholera and anthrax in sheep (1879-1881), and in 1885 a weakened-virus inoculation that saved a boy bitten by a rabid dog; Nature feature (https://media.nature.com/original/magazine-assets/d42859-020-00008-5/d42859-020-00008-5.pdf) on chicken cholera in 1879. 'Later' holds after the 1860s flask work. Pasteur worked with collaborators (e.g. Roux and Chamberland), but the lesson's 'hy het gemaak' is the usual attribution and not false at this level.

items.bewering: Daardie entstowwe het gewys dat 'n mens die verband kon gebruik om siekte te voorkom. Die verband was dus nie net 'n verklaring vir siekte nie.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory': the anthrax vaccine used germs weakened by heating; vaccinated sheep lived and unvaccinated sheep died. The lesson does not claim these were the first vaccines (Jenner's smallpox vaccine came earlier), only that they used the germ link.

items.bewering: Baie klein lewende dinge wat 'n mens siek kan maak. 'n Enkele kiem is te klein om met die blote oog te sien.
items.bron: Merriam-Webster Medical, 'germ'. Same wording as the study block, and it reads correctly on its own. See the study-block item for the viruses note.

items.bewering: Een soort baie klein lewende ding; sommige bakterieë is kieme wat siekte veroorsaak.
items.bron: Search summary from dictionary and educational sources: bacteria are single-celled living organisms found almost everywhere; Merriam-Webster lists bacteria as one kind of germ. 'Sommige' is correct: most bacteria do not cause disease.

items.bewering: 'n Manier waarop melk of 'n ander vloeistof warm gemaak word om die skadelike kieme daarin dood te maak.
items.bron: Britannica, 'pasteurization'; Wikipedia, 'Pasteurization': heat treatment of milk, wine, beer, juice and other liquids to destroy pathogens and spoilage organisms. 'Of 'n ander vloeistof' correctly covers its origin in wine.

items.bewering: 'n Middel wat 'n liggaam help om 'n bepaalde siekte later te weerstaan.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Germ Theory' (vaccines create immunity to a specific disease, e.g. anthrax and rabies); WHO, 'Rabies' fact sheet (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies) on vaccination before and after exposure. 'Help ... weerstaan' rightly does not promise full protection.

items.bewering: 'n Gevaarlike siekte wat meestal deur die byt van 'n siek dier oorgedra word.
items.bron: WHO, 'Rabies' fact sheet (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies): spreads via saliva, 'usually through bites, scratches, or direct contact with mucosa'; dogs are responsible in up to 99% of human cases; fatal once symptoms appear. 'Meestal' is accurate, because scratches and contact with saliva are rarer routes.

opsomming: All 28 checkable claims are confirmed, with nothing contradicted and nothing uncertain. The lesson has no true superlatives and no analogies, so the four priority or attribution claims (Pasteur did not discover germs, they were seen over a hundred years before him, he did not prove germ theory alone, and pasteurisation is named after him) are recorded as superlatives. All four hold. The one place a person might look twice is that 'kieme' calls germs 'lewende dinge', which includes viruses, whose status as living things is a matter of definition; the dictionary sense supports the wording, so it is not marked false.
